Surah 61 (al-Saff), Medinan, with 14 verses [revealed after al-Taghabun]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Limma: here the lam of possession (lam al-idafa) enters upon the interrogative ma (what?), just as other prepositions enter upon it in your saying: bima, fima, mimma, amma, ilam, alam (with what, in what, from what, about what, to what, for what). The alif is elided because ma and the preposition are treated as one word, and their use is very frequent in the speech of one who asks. The original form is used rarely, and one may pause on it with the added silent ha (ha' al-sakt) or with sukun (vowel-less pause). Whoever uses sukun in continuous recitation does so by treating it as if it were pausal, as is heard in the verse:

thalatha, arba'a (three, four), with the ha and with the vowel of the hamza thrown onto the preceding letter, which is elided.

This statement encompasses lying and breaking promises. It is narrated that the believers said, before they were commanded to fight: "If we knew which deeds are most beloved to Allah the Exalted, we would perform them and expend our wealth and our lives for them." So Allah the Exalted guided them to jihad in His cause, but they turned away on the day of Uhud, and He rebuked them. It has also been said: when Allah informed them of the reward of the martyrs of Badr, they said, "If we meet in battle, we will certainly exhaust our utmost effort in it," but they fled on the day of Uhud and did not fulfill it. It has also been said: a man would say, "I have killed," when he had not killed; "I have stabbed," when he had not stabbed; "I have struck," when he had not struck; "I have been patient," when he had not been patient. It has also been said: a certain man had harmed the Muslims and inflicted wounds upon them, and Suhayb killed him, but another man claimed his killing. Umar said to Suhayb, "Inform the Prophet, peace be upon him, that you killed him." He said, "I killed him only for Allah and His Messenger." Umar said, "O Messenger of Allah, Suhayb killed him." He said, "So it is, O Abu Yahya?" He said, "Yes." Then it was revealed [[Al-Tha'labi narrated it from the hadith of Suhayb, who said: "A man on the day of Badr had harmed the Muslims and inflicted wounds upon them, and Suhayb killed him. A man said, 'O Messenger of Allah, I killed so-and-so.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ was pleased by this. Then Amr ibn Abd al-Rahman said to Suhayb, 'Inform the Prophet ﷺ of that'..." - the hadith]] concerning the one who claimed it falsely. Al-Hasan said: it was revealed concerning the hypocrites. Their address with faith is mockery of them and of their faith. This is among the most eloquent and forceful speech.

[[Mahmud said: "This is among the most eloquent and forceful speech. Its meaning intends wonder without the form of wonder, to magnify the matter..." etc. Ahmad said: There is a fifth aspect beyond these four: his repetition of His saying "what you do not do," which is one word in one utterance. Among the benefits of repetition is awe and magnification; otherwise the statement would have been complete had it said, "Great is their hatred in the sight of Allah, that." Its repetition is only for the sake of this second benefit, and Allah knows best.]] in its meaning, intending wonder (ta'ajjub) without its verbal form, as in his saying:

"The fang of Kulayb has become red with its blood" [[The explanation of this witness was given earlier in volume three, page 273; refer to it if you wish. (Corrector's note)]]

The meaning of wonder is the magnification of the matter in the hearts of the listeners, because wonder arises only from something outside its kind and likeness. It is attributed to "that you say." Maqtan (hatred) is put in the accusative as a specification, indicating that their saying "what you do not do" is pure hatred with no admixture, due to the intensity of hatred in it. The word maqt was chosen because it is the most intense and most eloquent of hatred. From it comes the term nikah al-maqt (the hateful marriage), for contracting marriage upon the rabah [[His saying "upon the rabah" is with the ba' doubled, like al-dabbah. In al-Sihah: nikah al-maqt was in the pre-Islamic era: that a man marries his father's wife. (Corrector)]]. He did not limit himself to making the hatred great, but made it the most intense and most foul. "With Allah" is more forceful than that, for when the greatness of His hatred is established with Allah, its greatness and intensity are complete and doubts are removed from it. It is narrated from some of the early generations that he was asked, "Narrate to us," and he remained silent; then he was asked again, "Narrate to us," and he said, "You command me to say what I do not do, so you hasten the hatred of Allah."

In His saying, "Indeed Allah loves those who fight in His cause," following the mention of the hatred of the one who breaks his word, there is evidence [[Mahmud said: "His mention of this following the mention of the hatred of the one who breaks his word is evidence..." etc. Ahmad said: True. The first is a general preface to this particular story, like His saying, "O you who believe, do not put yourselves before Allah and His Messenger, and fear Allah; indeed Allah is Hearing and Knowing," and "O you who believe, do not raise your voices above the voice of the Prophet." The general prohibition came first, and the intent is that this particular matter is included within it, just as you say to one who has committed a specific offense: "Do not do what brings shame upon you, and do not revile Zayd." The benefit of such an arrangement is: the prohibition of one thing twice, once included in the general and once singled out in the specific, which is preferable to prohibiting it specifically twice, since that would be counted as repetition; and this repeats with what generalization carries of magnification and awe. Allah knows best.]] that the hatred has attached itself to the saying of those who promised steadfastness in fighting the disbelievers and did not fulfill it. Zayd ibn Ali recited "yuqatiluna" with a fatha on the ta'. It was also read "yuqtalun." "Saffan saffan" (in ranks): arranged in rows, or "saffin" with them arranged in rows, "ka-annahum" (as if they were) in their solid ranks, without gap or defect, "bunyanun" (a structure) whose parts are fitted and joined one to another. It has been said: it is permissible that it means the uniformity of their intentions in steadfastness, so that they are, in unity of word, like a solid, fitted structure. It is narrated from some of them: in it is evidence of the virtue of fighting on foot, because horsemen do not line up in this manner. His saying "saffan" and "ka-annahum bunyanun" are two overlapping circumstantial clauses [[Mahmud said: "His saying 'saffan, ka-annahum bunyanun marsus' are two overlapping circumstantial clauses." Ahmad said: He means that the meaning of the first includes the meaning of the second, because compactness is a condition of lining up, and Allah knows best.]].

Or it means: when he said to them what he said, such-and-such happened. ﴿تُؤْذُونَنِي﴾ ("you hurt me"): they harmed him in various ways, by belittling him and finding fault with him personally, by denying his signs, by disobeying him in matters where his benefit would return to them, by worshipping the calf, by asking to see God openly, and by denial, which is the neglect of God's right and his own right. ﴿وَقَدْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾ ("and you know well") is in the position of a circumstantial clause (al-hal), meaning: you hurt me while knowing with certain knowledge.

[[Mahmud said: "He showed that they were opposite to what is right, when he said: 'you hurt me while knowing…' etc." Ahmad said: The grammarians (ahl al-'Arabiyyah) say that "qad" accompanies the past tense to bring it close to the present. From this comes the caller's (mu'adhdhin's) saying: "The prayer has indeed been established." The accompaniment of the past tense also carries the sense of expectation, which is why Sibawayh said "qad fa'ala" is the answer to "lamma yaf'al." Al-Khalil said: this report is for people who are waiting for it. As for its use with the present tense, it conveys diminution, like "rubba" (perhaps), as in their saying: "Indeed the liar may (qad) tell the truth." If its meaning with the present tense is diminution, and it has entered the verse with a present-tense verb, then the correct view, and God knows best, is that this is from the kind of speech by which they intend exaggeration in what is reversed from it. In this sense "qad" is the counterpart of "rubba" in His saying: ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims﴾, for in this position it is more emphatic than "kam" in multiplication. Since "rubba" is used for multiplication in reversal of its original meaning of diminution, so too the use of "qad" here is to multiply their knowledge, meaning: its confirmation and emphasis in reversal of its original meaning of diminishing the original. And on this basis (the poet said):

"Indeed I leave the champion with his fingertips yellowed"

He praised himself for the frequency of this act from him, in reversal of his original habit. It should not be said that taking it in the verse to mean multiplication is impossible, because knowledge, being a connected thing, is neither multiplied nor diminished. We say: the firm establishment of an act, its realization, its emphasis, and its reaching the utmost limit in its kind is expressed by what is expressed by multiplication, and this is a sound expression. Do you not see that His saying ﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish﴾ belongs to this category, for what is meant is the intensity of their wish for that and its reaching its furthest extent, and nothing else. And God is the Granter of success.]] ﴿أَنِّي رَسُولُ اللَّهِ إِلَيْكُمْ﴾ ("that I am the messenger of God to you"). The consequence of your knowing this and its requirement is that you honour and revere me, not that you hurt me and disdain me, because whoever knows God and His greatness honours His messenger, knowing that honouring Him is in honouring His messenger; and because whoever hurts him, God's threat will certainly reach him.

﴿فَلَمَّا زاغُوا عن الحق أَزاغَ اللَّهُ قُلُوبَهُمْ﴾ ("So when they swerved from the truth, God caused their hearts to swerve"), by withholding His gracious favours (alutf) from them. The doctrine of the Ahl al-Sunnah (the people of the Sunnah) is that He, exalted is He, wills both evil and good, as has been established in its proper place. If you ask: what is the meaning of "qad" in His saying ﴿وَقَدْ تَعْلَمُونَ﴾? I say: its meaning is emphasis, as if He had said: "and you know with certain knowledge, with no doubt in it for you."

It is said: He said "O Children of Israel" and did not say "O people," as Moses had said, because he had no lineage among them that would make them his people. [Al-Zamakhshari said: "He only said 'O Children of Israel' and did not say 'O people' because he, may the blessings of God be upon our Prophet and upon him, had no lineage among them." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This is like His saying, ﴿When Shu'ayb said to them﴾, because Shu'ayb was not of the people to whom he was sent.]

The meaning is: I have been sent to you while confirming what came before me of the Torah, and while giving good news of a Messenger who will come after me. That is, my religion is the affirmation of the books of God and all of His prophets, those who came before and those who come after.

It is recited as "min ba'di" with the yā' sukūn and with the yā' fatḥa, and al-Khalil (al-Khalil ibn Ahmad) and Sibawayh (Sibawayh, the grammarian) preferred the fatḥa.

From Ka'b: The disciples (al-Hawariyyun) said to Jesus, "O Spirit of God, is there any community after us?" He said, "Yes, the community of Ahmad: wise, learned, righteous, and pious, as if they were prophets in their understanding. They are content from God with little provision, and God is content from them with little action."

If you ask: With what are "muşaddiqan" (confirming) and "mubashshiran" (giving good news) in the accusative? Is it by what is in "rasul" of the meaning of sending, or by "ilaykum"? I say: It is by the meaning of sending, because "ilaykum" is a complement of "rasul," so it cannot govern anything, since prepositions do not govern by themselves but by the meaning of a verb in them. When they occur as complements without implying a verb, how could they govern?

It is also recited as ﴿This is manifest magic﴾.

Who is more unjust than one who is called by his Lord, through the tongue of His Prophet, to Islam, which brings him the happiness of both abodes, yet who in return for answering it fabricates a lie against God, saying of the speech that calls His servants to the truth: "This is sorcery," because sorcery is falsehood and deception? Talha ibn Musarrif read *wa-huwa yud'a* (وهو يدعى), meaning *yud'a* (يدعى) in the sense of *yud'a* from *da'ahu* and *idda'ahu* (دعاه وادّعاه), as in *lamasahu* and *iltamasahu* (لمسه والتمسه). It is also reported from him as *yuddda'a* (يدّعى), in the sense of *yad'u* (يدعو), and the one who calls is God, Mighty and Majestic.

Origin: "They wish to extinguish," as it occurs in Surah Bara'ah (al-Tawbah). It is as if this lam (the lam of purpose) was added with the verb of wanting for emphasis, because it carries the sense of desire, as in your saying: "I came to you for the sake of honouring you" (ji'tuka li-ikramika). Likewise the lam is added in "la abaka" (may you have no father) for emphasis on the sense of the genitive construction in "la abaka" (without the lam: "la aba-ka"). As for "extinguishing the light of Allah with their mouths," it is a mockery of them in their wish to nullify Islam by their saying about the Qur'an, "This is sorcery." Their condition is depicted as that of one who blows into the light of the sun with his mouth in order to extinguish it. "And Allah will perfect His light" (wa-llahu mutimmu nurihi): that is, He will complete the truth and bring it to its utmost end. It is also read with the genitive construction (bi-l-idafah), "mutimmu nurih" (with the noun in the genitive, "mutimmu nuri-hi" as an idafah).

Wa-dīni l-ḥaqq (the religion of truth): the upright monotheistic creed (al-millah al-ḥanīfiyyah), "to make it prevail" (li-yuẓhirahu), that is, to make it supreme (li-yuʿliyahu) "over all religion" (ʿalā l-dīni kullihi), over all the religions that oppose it. By my life, he has indeed done so: no religion remains except that it is overcome and subdued by the religion of Islam.

And on the authority of Mujahid: when ʿIsa descends, there will be on earth only the religion of Islam. And it was read: "arsala nabiyyahu" (He sent His prophet).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 61, verses 10–13:

*Tunjikum* is read with both a light and a heavy form. *Tu'minun* is a resumption (*isti'naf*, a new sentence that answers an implied question), as if they had said: "How should we act?"

So it was said: ﴿You believe in God and His Messenger, and strive in God's way with your wealth and your selves.﴾ It is an informative statement with the meaning of a command, which is why it is answered by ﴿He will forgive you﴾. The reading of Ibn Mas'ud also supports this: "Believe in God and His Messenger, and strive."

[[Mahmud said: His words "*tu'minun*" are a resumption of speech. It is as though, when he had said the first statement, it was asked, "How shall we act?" and so it was said, "*You believe* ... etc."

Ahmad said: al-Farra's grammatical analysis, as mentioned, is only because if it were taken as the answer to ﴿Shall I direct you﴾, the meaning would be: if I direct you to such and such, I will forgive you. Then forgiveness would be conditional on the mere act of pointing them to good, and that is not the case. Forgiveness is conditional on their doing what they were directed to, not on the directing itself. Therefore he interpreted ﴿Shall I direct you﴾ as: "Will you trade in faith and jihad?" so that forgiveness is conditional on the act of faith and jihad, not on the directing. This interpretation is not needed. The essential meaning, once it is reduced to "Shall I direct you? I will forgive you," joins similar cases such as His words, ﴿Tell My servants who believe to establish prayer﴾, where the act of prayer is made conditional on the command to it, as if He said: "If you tell them to establish it, they will establish it."

Someone may object: "It has been said to some people, 'Establish prayer,' and they abandoned it." The answer is that the command directed at a believer firmly rooted in faith, since it is likely to be obeyed, is treated as if its fulfilment were certain and its reward were arranged upon it. Likewise here: since the directing of those who believe to good deeds is likely to be obeyed, and their obedience is a certain cause of forgiveness, it is treated as though obedience and forgiveness were both ensured by the directing. And God knows best.]] It is a statement in the sense of a command, and that is why it is answered by ﴿He will forgive you﴾.

It is indicated by the statement, "This is to announce the obligation to obey, as though he had obeyed, so he speaks of faith and jihad as already existing." Its parallel is the supplicant's saying, "May God forgive you" or "God will forgive you": the forgiveness is treated as already existing because of the strength of hope, as if it had already occurred and been realized.

If you ask: Does al-Farra's view that it answers ﴿Shall I direct you﴾ have any basis? I say: Its basis is that the object of the directing is the trade, and the trade is explained as faith and jihad. So it is as though it was said: "Will you trade in faith and jihad? He will forgive you." If you ask: What is the reading of Zayd ibn Ali, may God be pleased with them both, ﴿tu'minuna ... wa tujahidun﴾? I say: Its basis is that it is taken with an implied imperative *lam* (the jussive *lam*, "let"), as in the verse:

*Muhammad, may every soul be ransomed for you,*
*whenever you fear a calamity.*

It is attributed to Abu Talib, and some say to al-A'sha. He says: "O Messenger of God, may (every soul) be ransomed," meaning *li-tafda*, so the jussive *lam* of command has been omitted for the sake of poetic necessity. The context of the command justifies its omission. Otherwise, jussive particles, like prepositions, do not govern when omitted, except as an anomaly, as al-Sakkaki stated. The omission in a case like His words, ﴿Tell My servants who believe to establish prayer﴾, is easier, because its indicator is verbal, namely the word ﴿tell﴾ which signals a command. It has also been said that it is a statement with the meaning of supplication, lightened by dropping the *ya'*. It has also been said that this holds outside the rhyme-endings, and that the rhyme-ending is not correct. That is, "May God ransom you with every soul when you fear some calamity."

*Tabal* means *wabal* (calamity), its *waw* having been changed to *ta'*. It is also transmitted in the genitive case, as an attribute of *amr* (matter), but that is not good.]]

It is reported from Ibn Abbas that they said, "If we knew which deeds are most beloved to God, we would do them." Then this verse was revealed, but they remained for as long as God willed, saying, "Would that we knew what they are." So God guided them to it by His words, ﴿You believe﴾. This is evidence that ﴿You believe﴾ is a resumed statement, and that a command which comes upon souls after they have longed for it and looked forward to it has a stronger effect and is more readily accepted than one that catches them unprepared.

﴿That﴾, meaning what was mentioned of faith and jihad, ﴿is better for you than your wealth and your selves.﴾

If you ask: What is the meaning of His words, ﴿if you know﴾? I say: Its meaning is: if you know that it is better for you, it is better for you then. [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning: if you know that it is better for you, it is better for you then ..." Ahmad said: It seems that he takes the conditional on its literal sense, though this is not the apparent meaning, because their knowledge of this is certain, since the address is to the believers. The apparent meaning is that it belongs with His words, ﴿O you who believe, fear God and give up what remains of usury, if you are believers﴾. The purpose of this conditional is to alert them to the meaning that calls for obedience and to stir up zeal for obedience, as you say to someone whom you command to take revenge on his enemy, "If you are free, then avenge yourself," wanting only to stir up in him the zeal for vengeance. And God knows best.]] For when you know this and believe it, you will love faith and jihad more than you love your selves and your wealth, and so you will be sincere and prosper.

﴿And another [favour] you love: help from God and a near victory.﴾ Besides this mentioned blessing of forgiveness and reward in the hereafter, there is another blessing in this world that is beloved to you. Then He explained it by His words, ﴿help from God and a near victory﴾, that is, quick, and it is the conquest of Mecca. Al-Hasan said: it is the conquest of Persia and Byzantium. There is in ﴿you love it﴾ some reproach for loving what is immediate.

If you ask: To what does His words, ﴿and give good tidings to the believers﴾, connect? I say: To ﴿you believe﴾, because it has the meaning of a command, as if it was said: "Believe and strive, and God will protect you and help you, and give good tidings, O Messenger of God, to the believers of this." If you ask: Why did the one who read ﴿nasrun min Allah wa fathun qarib﴾ use the accusative? I say: It may be in the accusative by specification (*ikhtisas*), or as a complement of ﴿you will be helped with a help﴾ and ﴿He will open for you an opening﴾, or as a complement of: ﴿He will forgive you and admit you into gardens, and give you another [favour]: help from God and a near victory.﴾

Someone may object: "It has been said to some people, 'Establish prayer,' and they abandoned it." The answer is that the command directed at a believer firmly rooted in faith, since it is likely to be obeyed, is treated as if its fulfilment were certain and its reward were arranged upon it. Likewise here: since the directing of those who believe to good deeds is likely to be obeyed, and their obedience is a certain cause of forgiveness, it is treated as though obedience and forgiveness were both ensured by the directing. And God knows best.]] It is a statement in the sense of a command, and that is why it is answered by ﴿He will forgive you﴾.

It is indicated by the statement, "This is to announce the obligation to obey, as though he had obeyed, so he speaks of faith and jihad as already existing." Its parallel is the supplicant's saying, "May God forgive you" or "God will forgive you": the forgiveness is treated as already existing because of the strength of hope, as if it had already occurred and been realized.

If you ask: Does al-Farra's view that it answers ﴿Shall I direct you﴾ have any basis? I say: Its basis is that the object of the directing is the trade, and the trade is explained as faith and jihad. So it is as though it was said: "Will you trade in faith and jihad? He will forgive you." If you ask: What is the reading of Zayd ibn Ali, may God be pleased with them both, ﴿tu'minuna ... wa tujahidun﴾? I say: Its basis is that it is taken with an implied imperative *lam* (the jussive *lam*, "let"), as in the verse:

*Muhammad, may every soul be ransomed for you,*
*whenever you fear a calamity.*

It is attributed to Abu Talib, and some say to al-A'sha. He says: "O Messenger of God, may (every soul) be ransomed," meaning *li-tafda*, so the jussive *lam* of command has been omitted for the sake of poetic necessity. The context of the command justifies its omission. Otherwise, jussive particles, like prepositions, do not govern when omitted, except as an anomaly, as al-Sakkaki stated. The omission in a case like His words, ﴿Tell My servants who believe to establish prayer﴾, is easier, because its indicator is verbal, namely the word ﴿tell﴾ which signals a command. It has also been said that it is a statement with the meaning of supplication, lightened by dropping the *ya'*. It has also been said that this holds outside the rhyme-endings, and that the rhyme-ending is not correct. That is, "May God ransom you with every soul when you fear some calamity."

*Tabal* means *wabal* (calamity), its *waw* having been changed to *ta'*. It is also transmitted in the genitive case, as an attribute of *amr* (matter), but that is not good.]]

It is reported from Ibn Abbas that they said, "If we knew which deeds are most beloved to God, we would do them." Then this verse was revealed, but they remained for as long as God willed, saying, "Would that we knew what they are." So God guided them to it by His words, ﴿You believe﴾. This is evidence that ﴿You believe﴾ is a resumed statement, and that a command which comes upon souls after they have longed for it and looked forward to it has a stronger effect and is more readily accepted than one that catches them unprepared.

﴿That﴾, meaning what was mentioned of faith and jihad, ﴿is better for you than your wealth and your selves.﴾

If you ask: What is the meaning of His words, ﴿if you know﴾? I say: Its meaning is: if you know that it is better for you, it is better for you then. [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning: if you know that it is better for you, it is better for you then ..." Ahmad said: It seems that he takes the conditional on its literal sense, though this is not the apparent meaning, because their knowledge of this is certain, since the address is to the believers. The apparent meaning is that it belongs with His words, ﴿O you who believe, fear God and give up what remains of usury, if you are believers﴾. The purpose of this conditional is to alert them to the meaning that calls for obedience and to stir up zeal for obedience, as you say to someone whom you command to take revenge on his enemy, "If you are free, then avenge yourself," wanting only to stir up in him the zeal for vengeance. And God knows best.]] For when you know this and believe it, you will love faith and jihad more than you love your selves and your wealth, and so you will be sincere and prosper.

﴿And another [favour] you love: help from God and a near victory.﴾ Besides this mentioned blessing of forgiveness and reward in the hereafter, there is another blessing in this world that is beloved to you. Then He explained it by His words, ﴿help from God and a near victory﴾, that is, quick, and it is the conquest of Mecca. Al-Hasan said: it is the conquest of Persia and Byzantium. There is in ﴿you love it﴾ some reproach for loving what is immediate.

If you ask: To what does His words, ﴿and give good tidings to the believers﴾, connect? I say: To ﴿you believe﴾, because it has the meaning of a command, as if it was said: "Believe and strive, and God will protect you and help you, and give good tidings, O Messenger of God, to the believers of this." If you ask: Why did the one who read ﴿nasrun min Allah wa fathun qarib﴾ use the accusative? I say: It may be in the accusative by specification (*ikhtisas*), or as a complement of ﴿you will be helped with a help﴾ and ﴿He will open for you an opening﴾, or as a complement of: ﴿He will forgive you and admit you into gardens, and give you another [favour]: help from God and a near victory.﴾

Readings: "Be helpers of God" and "be helpers of God" (with the second word indefinite, وأنصارا لله). Ibn Mas'ud read: "Be you helpers of God." This carries an added emphasis on the obligation of helping them against their enemies. If you ask: what is the correct basis for the comparison, when its apparent meaning is comparing their being helpers with the words of Jesus, peace be upon him: "Who are my helpers in the cause of God?" [[Mahmud said: "If you ask, what is the basis of the comparison, and its apparent meaning is comparing their being helpers ... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: a fine statement and a completion of what is best: that one should distinguish between the two idafa constructions mentioned, namely that the first is pure (mahda) and the second is not pure (ghayr mahda), so be attentive to this. God is the Granter of success.]]? I answer: the comparison is to be understood in terms of meaning, and on this basis it is valid. The intended meaning is: be helpers of God just as the disciples (al-Hawariyyun) were helpers of Jesus when he said to them, "Who are my helpers in the cause of God?" If you ask: what is the meaning of his saying "Who are my helpers in the cause of God?" I answer: its meaning must correspond to the disciples' reply, "We are helpers of God." What corresponds to it is that the meaning is: "Who is my companion, heading towards the support of God?" The construction "my helpers" (ansari) differs from the construction "helpers of God" (ansar Allah), for the meaning of "We are helpers of God" is: "We are those who help God." And the meaning of "Who are my helpers?" is: "Who among the helpers are specially devoted to me and will be with me in supporting God?" It is not valid that its meaning be: "Who will help me alongside God?", because that does not correspond to the reply. The evidence for this is the reading of one who read: "min ansar Allah" (who are the helpers of God?). The Hawariyyun (disciples) were his chosen companions (asfiya'uhu), and they were the first to believe in him, and they were twelve men. The hawari of a man is his chosen one and his pure essence (khalsanuhu), from al-hawr, which is pure whiteness. [[His statement "and his khalsanuhu" means his pure essence; it applies to both singular and plural, as in al-Sihah. In it also: al-darmak is fine flour; and al-hawwari is the flour that has been whitened (hawwar min al-ta'am, i.e., whitened). And in it too: al-hawwari is fine white bread flour, and all of these are with a damma vowel, as al-Sihah states. (Ibn al-Munayyir)]] Al-hawwari means fine wheat flour. From it is the saying of the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him: "Al-Zubayr is my cousin and my hawari from my community." [[Narrated by al-Nasa'i from the hadith of Jabir. It is in the two Sahihs with the wording: "Every prophet has a hawari, and my hawari is al-Zubayr."]] It is also said that they were launderers who whitened clothes. A parallel to hawari in its form is al-hawali, meaning one with many tricks. "A group of them believed in Jesus, and a group disbelieved in him, so We strengthened those who believed against their enemies, and they became dominant over them." It is related from Zayd ibn Ali that their dominance was by argument (bi'l-hujja).

From the Messenger of God, peace and blessings be upon him: "Whoever recites Surat al-Saff, Jesus will send blessings upon him and seek forgiveness for him for as long as he is in the world, and on the Day of Resurrection he will be his companion." [[Narrated by al-Tha'labi, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Wahidi from the hadith of Ubayy ibn Ka'b, may God be pleased with him.]]
